newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada dollar weakness a test for Bank of Canada.
newsitem.headline: Canada dollar weakness a test for Bank of Canada.

text.p: Recent weakening in the Canadian dollar is a probe of the Bank of Canada's monetary policy as investors test the central bank's resolve by selling the currency.
The selling has driven down the Monetary Conditions Index (MCI), the Bank of Canada's economic measure for determining the appropriate level of domestic interest rates.
"For the time being a test of the Bank of Canada's credibility seems to be dominating market action," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Canada.
The Canadian dollar on Thursday weakened to around C$1.3760 (US$0.7267) -- its lowest levels since early August -- from the year's high of C$1.3291 reached in November.
Economists said big market players have been weakening the currency to probe whether the Bank of Canada will raise its short-term interest rate targets.

The Bank of Canada last cut the ceiling of its 50 basis point target operating band for the overnight rate to 3.25 percent from 3.50 percent on November 8. The central bank said it slashed rates to prevent a tightening in the monetary conditions index as a result of a stronger dollar.
"These declines in rates have offset the effect on monetary conditions of further movement of the Canadian dollar to a new, higher trading range," the central bank said in its November 8 statement.
Since the cut, the Bank of Canada's monetary conditions index has fallen 80 basis points, prompting some market players to call for a rise in interest rates if the Bank of Canada is to be consistent.
Since November 8 the index, which is a complex mix of interest rates, bonds and currencies has fallen to -6.0114 from -5.2125 on November 8.

"If they (the Bank of Canada) were so locked into the MCI when the currency was strengthening that it forced them to lower rates each time (it rose), well when does the point come that easing MCI requires an offsetting rate hike?" said Anita Lauria, economist at Salomon Brothers in New York.
Lauria sees purchasing power parity for the Canadian dollar around C$1.1800 (US$0.8474), but she predicted it will only strengthen to C$1.2800 (US$0.7812) this year.
Most economists said they expect the currency to strengthen this year, reflecting the improving economy, narrowing budget deficit and a current account surplus.
"The currency is undervalued right now, but as long as there is some uncertainty about policy and there is some question about the Bank of Canada's resolve, you will see it undervalued," Lauria said.
Economists said the Bank of Canada is unlikely to raise rates in response to this particular challenge, given that its one to three percent target range for inflation is not likely to be threatened.

"What questions the Bank's credibility at the end of the day is whether or not it meets its inflation targets," said Duetche's Spence. "And at the moment I would think that it's fairly safe to say that inflation is not going to move out of the one to three percent target range for the next couple of years, so I don't see this as targeting the Bank's credibility at this point."
((Paul Casciato, Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8100 or email: paul.casciato@reuters.com))
